# Concepts

Every question is tagged with one or more of these 62 concepts. The first tag on a question is the concept it tests most directly. Counts include every question that carries the tag.

Jump to a group: [Inside the model](#inside-the-model) | [Context](#context) | [Training](#training) | [Reasoning and choosing a model](#reasoning-and-choosing-a-model) | [Agents](#agents) | [Agent skills](#agent-skills) | [Decisions, evaluation and feedback](#decisions-evaluation-and-feedback) | [Practice and course context](#practice-and-course-context)

## Inside the model

| Concept | Tag | Questions | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Decoder transformer pipeline](#transformer-pipeline) | `transformer-pipeline` | 8 | The end-to-end path from context to next token: tokenize, embed, pass through the decoder stacks, produce probabilities, pick a token. The same basic architecture sits under Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. |
| [Tokenization](#tokenization) | `tokenization` | 14 | Splitting text into tokens drawn from a fixed vocabulary and replacing each with its token ID (a number). |
| [Token](#token) | `token` | 5 | The unit a model reads and writes: a whole word, a piece of a word, or a symbol. Models predict tokens, not words. |
| [Token embedding](#token-embedding) | `token-embedding` | 22 | The learned vector (a long list of numbers) that a token ID is mapped to before the decoder stacks. One fixed embedding per token, whatever the sentence. |
| [Semantic space](#semantic-space) | `semantic-space` | 12 | The high-dimensional space embeddings live in, where location is meaning: related tokens sit near each other and directions can carry relationships (king - man + woman lands near queen). |
| [Attention](#attention) | `attention` | 32 | The part of each decoder stack that lets a token gather information from the other tokens in the context, moving its representation toward its meaning in this particular sentence. |
| [MLP (multi-layer perceptron)](#mlp) | `mlp` | 28 | The feed-forward part of each decoder stack. Its learned weights hold a compressed, lossy picture of the world (the "fuzzy JPEG") that it applies to each token's representation. |
| [Decoder stack](#decoder-stack) | `decoder-stack` | 15 | One block of attention followed by an MLP. A model runs many stacks in sequence, each refining the representation further. |
| [Activation space](#activation-space) | `activation-space` | 7 | The changing internal representations (activations) of tokens as they move through the stacks. Unlike the fixed token embedding, these depend on the context. |
| [Recurrent depth (looping)](#recurrent-depth) | `recurrent-depth` | 15 | Running the same decoder stack or block more than once so a representation gets another pass ("a second bite of the apple"), adding computation without adding parameters. |
| [Probability distribution over tokens](#probability-distribution-over-tokens) | `probability-distribution-over-tokens` | 13 | The model's output at each step: a probability for every token in its vocabulary (the softmax at the end of the pipeline). |
| [Next-token prediction](#next-token-prediction) | `next-token-prediction` | 15 | The single job a language model is trained to do and does at run time: predict what token comes next given the context. |
| [Sampling and temperature](#sampling-and-temperature) | `sampling-and-temperature` | 19 | How one token is chosen from the probability distribution. Temperature reshapes the distribution: higher means more varied, lower means more predictable. |
| [Autoregression](#autoregression) | `autoregression` | 13 | Generating one token at a time and feeding each chosen token back into the context for the next step, so every choice shapes what follows. |
| [Parameter](#parameter) | `parameter` | 18 | A single learned number (weight) in the model. The parameter count is how many there are; they are fixed once training ends. |
| [Model size](#model-size) | `model-size` | 26 | How big a model is (parameter count, width of the embedding space, number of decoder stacks) and what bigger does and does not buy you. |
| [Learned knowledge](#learned-knowledge) | `learned-knowledge` | 23 | What a model knows from training and how it is stored: compressed and approximate, not a searchable database of facts or a copy of its sources. |
| [Hallucination](#hallucination) | `hallucination` | 10 | Fluent output that is wrong. The model always produces the likely-sounding continuation; sometimes likely-sounding is not true. |

## Context

| Concept | Tag | Questions | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Context](#context) | `context` | 30 | Everything the model sees for a given step: system instructions, the conversation so far, uploaded files, tool results and its own output so far. The most important lever you have. |
| [Context length](#context-length) | `context-length` | 5 | The maximum number of tokens a model can hold in its context at once (the context window), and what happens as you approach it. |
| [Grounding with documents](#grounding) | `grounding` | 9 | Putting the relevant source material into the context so the answer draws on it rather than on the model's lossy memory, and why irrelevant material does not help. |

## Training

| Concept | Tag | Questions | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Pre-training](#pre-training) | `pre-training` | 13 | The first, largest training stage: next-token prediction over a huge body of text (and sometimes images), producing a base model. |
| [Self-supervised learning](#self-supervised-learning) | `self-supervised-learning` | 12 | Training where the answer key comes from the data itself, such as hiding the next token and asking the model to guess it. |
| [Post-training](#post-training) | `post-training` | 15 | Training after pre-training that turns a base model into an assistant: supervised fine-tuning on example responses, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and similar methods. |
| [Alignment](#alignment) | `alignment` | 5 | Work to make a model's behavior helpful, honest and safe, such as refusing harmful requests, and why that behavior is never perfectly reliable. |
| [Training vs. inference](#training-vs-inference) | `training-vs-inference` | 11 | Training changes the weights; inference (using the model) does not. A model can respond differently to new context without learning anything. |

## Reasoning and choosing a model

| Concept | Tag | Questions | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Thinking / reasoning](#thinking-reasoning) | `thinking-reasoning` | 38 | A model generating hidden tokens that work through a problem before its visible answer. Same architecture and same next-token mechanism, just more tokens spent first. |
| [Thinking budget and effort](#thinking-budget) | `thinking-budget` | 27 | The limit on how many thinking tokens a model may spend (the effort setting in Claude), and matching that budget to the task. |
| [Choosing a model](#model-selection) | `model-selection` | 23 | Picking a model tier (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, Fable, or another vendor's equivalents): the smallest model that does the job correctly. |
| [Inference speed and hardware](#inference-speed) | `inference-speed` | 14 | How fast tokens are produced (GPUs, specialized chips, local laptops) and why taking in a prompt is faster than writing an answer. |
| [KV cache](#kv-cache) | `kv-cache` | 1 | The stored attention keys and values for tokens already processed, so each new token does not recompute the whole context. |
| [Cost, usage and footprint](#cost-and-usage) | `cost-and-usage` | 13 | Usage limits and credits, and the energy and environmental cost of bigger models and bigger budgets. |
| [Multimodality](#multimodality) | `multimodality` | 8 | Models that work with images, audio or video as well as text, whether trained jointly (native) or given a separate adapter. |
| [History of AI](#ai-history) | `ai-history` | 5 | The eras of AI (problem solvers, expert systems, machine learning, deep learning) and where transformers, generative AI and agents fit. |
| [AGI (artificial general intelligence)](#agi) | `agi` | 5 | What AGI has been taken to mean, how definitions and levels frameworks differ, and the argument about whether a milestone has passed. |

## Agents

| Concept | Tag | Questions | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Agent](#agent) | `agent` | 24 | A model plus tools plus autonomy: a system that can take actions in a loop toward a goal, not just reply once. |
| [Chat vs. agent](#chat-vs-agent) | `chat-vs-agent` | 6 | The difference between a plain chat and an agent surface (Cowork, Claude Code): same model, different access, tools and ability to act. |
| [Harness](#harness) | `harness` | 20 | The software around the model that manages context, carries out tool calls, enforces permissions and returns results. The model proposes; the harness executes. |
| [Tool](#tool) | `tool` | 21 | A capability the harness can run on the model's behalf, such as reading a file, running a command or searching, with the result returned into context. |
| [Connector (MCP)](#connector) | `connector` | 2 | An add-on that gives an agent access to an outside system, often through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). |
| [File system](#file-system) | `file-system` | 10 | The folders and files an agent can read and write, and why working through files lets an agent handle projects bigger than its context. |
| [Memory](#memory) | `memory` | 10 | How information persists beyond one context window: notes, working records, remembered preferences and project files, and keeping them accurate. |
| [Context management](#context-management) | `context-management` | 9 | Keeping a long task's context useful: compaction and summaries, starting fresh chats, and keeping original evidence available. |
| [Subagent](#subagent) | `subagent` | 5 | A fresh agent given a focused assignment and just the background it needs, so it starts with a clean context. |
| [Permissions and safety](#permissions-and-safety) | `permissions-and-safety` | 12 | What an agent is allowed to do (access controls, sandboxes, approvals) and judging whether shared code or broad access is safe. |
| [Computer use](#computer-use) | `computer-use` | 4 | Agents that operate a computer's screen, mouse and keyboard, and why that remains hard. |
| [Directing an agent](#task-specification) | `task-specification` | 22 | Telling an agent what you need: stating the problem and goal (a "North Star"), constraints and acceptance criteria rather than step-by-step instructions. |
| [Verification](#verification) | `verification` | 33 | Checking that work actually happened and is correct (reading back the result, inspecting the file) rather than trusting a claim that it did. |

## Agent skills

| Concept | Tag | Questions | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Agent skill](#agent-skill) | `agent-skill` | 17 | A folder of reusable instructions (and optionally scripts and references) that an agent loads when a task calls for it. |
| [Skill structure](#skill-structure) | `skill-structure` | 35 | What goes in a skill folder: SKILL.md with its name and description, references/, scripts/, assets/, and what stays loaded versus loaded on demand. |
| [Skill selection](#skill-selection) | `skill-selection` | 16 | How an agent decides which skill to use from its name and description, and how vague, overlapping or conflicting skills go wrong. |
| [Skill scope](#skill-scope) | `skill-scope` | 3 | Where a skill lives and who can use it: a personal skill that follows you across projects versus a project skill tied to one project's conventions. |
| [Skill Creator](#skill-creator) | `skill-creator` | 7 | The skill for building, improving and testing other skills. |
| [Evaluating a skill](#skill-evaluation) | `skill-evaluation` | 24 | Testing whether a skill helps: comparing runs with and without it on the same inputs, criteria set in advance, varied test cases, the cheaper model it will run on. |
| [Sharing skills](#skill-sharing) | `skill-sharing` | 10 | Moving skills between people and hosts: repositories, READMEs, portability across providers, and what breaks when a skill is copied. |

## Decisions, evaluation and feedback

| Concept | Tag | Questions | What it means |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Classification and decision models](#classification) | `classification` | 0 | Choosing among fixed options (labels) rather than writing open-ended text, and when a specialized decision model fits better. |
| [Calibration](#calibration) | `calibration` | 0 | Whether stated probabilities match how often things actually happen: of events given 80%, about 80% should occur. |
| [Decisions under risk](#decision-under-risk) | `decision-under-risk` | 0 | Combining probabilities with costs (false alarms, misses, what each outcome costs) to choose an action, not just the most likely outcome. |
| [Feedback and rubrics](#feedback-and-rubrics) | `feedback-and-rubrics` | 2 | Grading against a rubric and writing feedback that names what was missed and how to fix it. |
